name: Banana peel
explanation: Fruit peels are kitchen waste and compost easily.

name: Apple core
explanation: Leftover fruit is biodegradable kitchen waste.

name: Vegetable peels
explanation: Peels and trimmings go straight into wet waste.

name: Leftover rice
explanation: Cooked food scraps are wet waste.

name: Onion peels
explanation: Dry-looking, but onion skins are plant matter and compost fine.

name: Stale bread
explanation: Old bread is food waste, so it belongs in wet waste.

name: Leftover dal
explanation: Cooked food is wet waste. Drain excess liquid first.

name: Mango seed
explanation: Fruit seeds and stones are biodegradable.

name: Watermelon rind
explanation: Fruit rinds are wet kitchen waste.

name: Potato peel
explanation: Peels are biodegradable kitchen waste.

name: Dry leaves
explanation: Garden waste is biodegradable, even when it is dry.

name: Corn cob
explanation: Corn cobs are plant matter and compost slowly but surely.

name: Orange peel
explanation: Citrus peels are wet waste.

name: Cucumber peel
explanation: Vegetable scraps are wet waste.

name: Used tea leaves
explanation: Loose tea leaves are biodegradable and great for compost.

name: Spoiled tomato
explanation: Rotten produce is wet waste.

name: Grape stems
explanation: Fruit stems are plant matter and compost easily.

name: Newspaper
explanation: Clean paper is dry waste and is easy to recycle.

name: Plastic bottle
explanation: Empty plastic bottles are dry, recyclable waste.

name: Cardboard box
explanation: Flatten cardboard and put it in dry waste for recycling.

name: Glass jar
explanation: Rinse jars and put them in dry waste.

name: Tin can
explanation: Metal cans are dry waste. Rinse them first.

name: Old notebook
explanation: Paper and notebooks are dry, recyclable waste.

name: Plastic bag
explanation: Plastic bags are dry waste. Keep them clean and dry.

name: Old T-shirt
explanation: Textiles are dry waste. Donate them if still wearable.

name: Worn-out shoe
explanation: Shoes are made of rubber, fabric and plastic: dry waste.

name: Ballpoint pen
explanation: Plastic and metal pens are dry waste.

name: Old toothbrush
explanation: Plastic bristles and handle make it dry waste.

name: Envelope
explanation: Paper envelopes are dry, recyclable waste.

name: Magazine
explanation: Glossy paper is still dry waste.

name: Broken plastic toy
explanation: Plastic toys are dry waste. Remove any batteries first.

name: Bent steel spoon
explanation: Metal is dry waste and is valuable to scrap dealers.

name: Soda can
explanation: Aluminium cans are dry waste and highly recyclable.

name: Leftover paint tin
explanation: Paint contains solvents and chemicals. Keep it out of dry waste.

name: Rat poison
explanation: Poisons are hazardous to people, pets and soil.

name: Used syringe
explanation: Needles can injure waste workers. Cap it and keep it separate.

name: Pesticide can
explanation: Pesticide residue is toxic, even in an empty can.

name: Toilet cleaner with leftover liquid
explanation: Strong acids and chemicals are domestic hazardous waste.
note: A fully empty, rinsed bottle can go in dry waste.

name: Eggshells
explanation: Shells feel hard but are biodegradable and add calcium to compost.

name: Coconut shell
explanation: Coconut shells are plant matter. They are slow to compost, but still wet waste.
note: Some cities collect coconut shells separately.

name: Chips packet
explanation: Multi-layer plastic is dry waste, even with crumbs inside.

name: Broken glass
explanation: Glass is dry waste. Wrap the shards in paper and label it 'sharp'.

name: Coffee grounds
explanation: Used coffee grounds are biodegradable and great for compost.

name: Peanut shells
explanation: Nut shells are plant matter, so they are wet waste.

name: Fish bones
explanation: Fish scraps and bones are biodegradable food waste.

name: Greasy pizza box
explanation: Soiled cardboard is still dry waste. Scrape off any food first.
note: Food-soiled paper is hard to recycle.

name: Takeaway container
explanation: Rinse plastic food containers and put them in dry waste.

name: Aluminium foil
explanation: Foil is metal, so it is dry waste. Wipe off any food.

name: Bubble wrap
explanation: Packaging plastic is dry waste.

name: Thermocol packaging
explanation: Thermocol (polystyrene) is plastic, so it goes in dry waste.

name: Old phone charger
explanation: Electronics are e-waste. Keep them out of dry waste.
note: Best given to an authorised e-waste collector.

name: Nail polish bottle
explanation: Nail polish contains solvents, which makes it hazardous waste.

name: Hair dye tube
explanation: Hair dye chemicals can contaminate water and soil.

name: Empty toothpaste tube
explanation: The tube is plastic and foil laminate: dry waste.

name: Old CD
explanation: CDs are polycarbonate plastic with a thin metal layer: dry waste.

name: Broken ceramic mug
explanation: Ceramics do not break down. Wrap the pieces and put them in dry waste.

name: Leftover curry
explanation: Cooked food, including meat curry, is wet waste.

name: Empty milk pouch
explanation: Rinse milk pouches and put them in dry waste. Leftover milk attracts pests.

name: Aerosol spray can
explanation: Pressurised cans can explode and may hold chemical residue.

name: Used tea bag
explanation: Tea bags are wet waste. Remove the staple and string tag first.
note: Some tea bags contain plastic mesh.

name: Rubber band
explanation: Rubber bands are dry waste.

name: Used sanitary pad
explanation: Wrap it in newspaper and put it in dry waste. Many cities also run separate sanitary collection.

name: Used diaper
explanation: Wrap it in newspaper and put it in dry waste, or use your city's sanitary collection.

name: Thermal paper receipt
explanation: Its chemical coating makes it unsuitable for paper recycling, but it is still dry waste.

name: Tetra pack (juice carton)
explanation: Layers of paper, plastic and foil; rinse and flatten it for dry waste.

name: Dead AA battery
explanation: Contains metals that leach into soil. Never in dry waste.

name: CFL bulb or tube light
explanation: Contains mercury. Keep it unbroken and separate.

name: Expired medicines
explanation: Chemicals can pollute water. Many pharmacies take them back.

name: Mosquito repellent refill
explanation: The liquid is an insecticide.

name: Puja flowers
explanation: Fully biodegradable; remove any plastic or thread first.

name: Chicken bones
explanation: Biodegradable, though slow to compost.

name: Silica gel packet
explanation: Not food, not hazardous at home.

name: Empty medicine strip
explanation: An empty foil strip is dry waste. Only leftover tablets are hazardous.

name: Broken mercury thermometer
explanation: Mercury is highly toxic. Seal it in a container and keep it separate.

name: Watch battery
explanation: Tiny button cells contain mercury or lithium. They are hazardous.

name: Used paper cup
explanation: A thin plastic lining stops it composting, so it is dry waste.

name: Wet wipes
explanation: Despite the name, wipes contain plastic fibres. They are dry waste.

name: Chewing gum
explanation: Gum is made from a synthetic rubber base, so it does not biodegrade.

name: Old mobile phone
explanation: Phones contain a lithium battery and heavy metals. Treat them as hazardous e-waste.
note: Best given to an authorised e-waste collector.

name: Cigarette butt
explanation: The filter is plastic (cellulose acetate). Stub it out fully and put it in dry waste.

name: Used razor blade
explanation: Wrap blades in thick paper so they can't cut anyone, then put them in dry waste.
note: Some cities collect blades with sanitary waste.
